title: Ancient Japanese Communities Found Ways to Adapt After a Huge Eruption
summary:
About 7,300 years ago, the Kikai-Akahoya volcano erupted beneath the sea near Japan. At that time, Japan was home to Jomon communities, people who lived by hunting and gathering. The eruption caused earthquakes and large waves and covered the land with thick volcanic ash.

For years, archaeologists, scientists who study past human life, have disagreed about what happened to the people living nearby. Some thought the people almost completely disappeared. Others thought some communities survived close to the disaster.

A new study led by Lund University in Sweden found that the real story was a mix of both. "The disaster caused major loss of life. However, survivors migrated, forged new social relations, innovated new kinds of economy," said lead author Enrico Crema of Cambridge University.

The researchers found that different regions responded in different ways. In southern Kyushu, an island in Japan, the population had already been shrinking before the eruption. In northern Kyushu, the population had been growing, and that growth continued afterward. People fleeing the worst-hit areas may have moved there. Survivors who lived inland also seem to have moved toward the northern coast, where sea life recovered quickly and provided food.

The team also found surprising changes far from the volcano. Places that had been growing before the eruption stopped growing or shrank afterward. The researchers say the eruption may have briefly disrupted the climate. Another possible reason is that deer and wild boar, important foods for the Jomon, may have worn down their teeth grazing on ash-covered land.

Professor Peter Jordan of Lund University said the study shows that even in very hard situations, communities "need to adjust, collaborate, and find new connections." The findings suggest a big disaster can affect people far beyond the place where it happens.
why_it_matters: The study shows that people can respond to a huge disaster in many different ways, and that a catastrophe can affect places far from where it strikes. Understanding this helps us think about how communities recover today.

keywords.explanation: Archaeologists are scientists who study how people lived long ago by examining the things they left behind.
The Jomon were ancient people of Japan who lived by hunting, fishing and gathering.
Volcanic ash is tiny pieces of rock and glass blasted into the air by an eruption.
Migrated means moved from one place to live in another.
A population is the number of people living in a place.

background_read: An undersea volcano erupts beneath the ocean, and a large one can cause earthquakes, huge waves and widespread ash.
Japan is a chain of islands, and Kyushu is one of its main islands in the south.
The Jomon were early people of Japan who lived by hunting, fishing and gathering, so damage to forests, animals and the sea directly affected their food.
Archaeologists estimate how populations rose or fell by studying the remains people left behind at many sites.
